lesson.title: A Perfect Split Step Can Be Late
lesson.hook: Your split step looks correct, yet the first move still begins after the ball is gone.
lesson.tomorrow: Next time you rally, sync your split to their strike and land ready to push as direction appears.

pro.label: What the split step buys
pro.moment: In a lab study of a simulated tennis reaction task, participants reached the target faster when they split-stepped: 764 ms on average, against 868 ms without.
pro.read: About a tenth of a second, bought with timing, not speed.

drill.name: Land on "hit"
drill.how: Your partner feeds from both sides. Say "hit" out loud as they strike the ball, and land your split on the word. Twenty balls, then rally.

steps.name: Land, settle, then go
steps.sit: You reach your spot. Watch the split step and your first move.
opts: The split carries you off line
You land, then pause before moving
You push off while still in the air
steps.payoff: You landed too early, then had to start again.
steps.principle: Land as their shot becomes readable, so the landing turns into your first step.
steps.why: Here you land well before they hit, settle, and restart. Landing just after their contact lets the landing feed the first push.
steps.take: Watch LAND, then THEIR HIT: land too early and you have to start again.

lines.A: The split lands where it started — it doesn't carry you off line.
lines.B: Right — you land, settle, and only then start again. That pause costs time.
lines.C: Both feet are down before you go — the push isn't in the air.
lines.D: Moving after their hit is normal. The pause before it isn't.

steps.name: Land just after the hit
steps.sit: Same spot, same shot. Watch what changes.
opts: A quicker push from the same landing
steps.payoff: You land just after their hit and go as the ball becomes readable.
steps.principle: Time the landing to their contact, not to your own rhythm.
steps.why: Nothing else changed: same spot, same push. Landing just after their hit means there's no settled pause.
steps.take: Land just after their hit and push as it becomes readable.

lines.A: The landing is no wider — only its timing moved.
lines.B: The push isn't quicker — it just starts sooner after the hit.
lines.C: Right — you land just after their hit, so there's no pause.
lines.D: Same spot as before — only the timing changed.

steps.name: Their shorter swing
steps.sit: They shorten their swing. With your old rhythm, the ball gets past you.
steps.q: What do you change on the next ball?
opts: Wait to see where it goes
steps.payoff: A quicker swing needs an earlier split, not a harder push.
steps.principle: Match your split to their swing, whatever its speed.
steps.why: Their shorter swing brings the hit forward. Starting the same split sooner puts your landing back on their contact; pushing harder or splitting smaller can't win back the time.
steps.take: A quicker swing? Start the same split sooner, so you land as they hit.

lines.A: Waiting for the direction, then splitting — the ball is past you.
lines.B: A smaller split pushes weaker — the ball gets past you.
lines.C: Still landing late — a harder push can't make it up.
lines.D: Split a beat sooner — you land as it's readable and get there.
